stories.text: The church of St Ann was begun for the new district in the 1860s: Sydney Pierrepont, 3rd Earl Manvers, laid its foundation stone on 23 September 1863, and it was consecrated on 26 September 1864, a daughter church of St Mary's. The parish church today is St Ann with Emmanuel. Whether the 1864 church stood here is not known.

236801.sum: St Ann with Emmanuel is a church.

stories.text: Edward VI granted the land on Hunger Hill to the Corporation of Nottingham in 1551. In 1604–05 it was enclosed and let in plots to 30 burgesses and their widows, an arrangement that lasted until 1842.

In the 1830s the Clay Fields were divided into plots, and the gardens on Hunger Hill became the St Ann's Allotments, the oldest and largest allotment site in England.[^s1] Hungerhill Gardens alone has 456 plots over about 52 acres, with sheds and summerhouses from the 19th century; the whole site is listed Grade II*.[^s2]

241948.sum: St Anns Allotments Visitor Centre is an office building on Ransom Road.

stories.text: Until the Inclosure Act of 1845 the area was open Clay Fields. The Act let the town take 1,068 acres for housing, and by 1880 the streets of terraced houses called New Town were complete. The terraces north of Victoria Park are listed, as a once common kind of house now mostly lost to bombs and clearance.

298577.sum: 1 to 30, the Promenade is a terrace of houses on Promenade. The building dates from about 1860, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II listed.
